title: Cambridge International AS & A Level Geography (9696)

officialDocument.title: Cambridge International AS & A Level Geography 9696 syllabus for 2027, 2028 and 2029 (version 1, published September 2024)
officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Topic and sub-topic headings (1 Hydrology, river processes and hazards ... 14.3 Monitoring and response to pathogenic diseases) are transcribed with their printed numbers; objective codes are the printed content-heading references (topic, sub-topic, heading, e.g. 1.1.4, with a suffix a or b where one heading yields two objectives). Objectives paraphrase the content in our own words. The three sections (AS, A, SK) and the skills topic S (S1-S3) are ours, summarising the geographical skills, resource skills and assessment objectives sections. No syllabus text is reproduced.
notes: Source (read 2026-10-08): the official PDF 'Cambridge International AS & A Level Geography 9696 syllabus for 2027, 2028 and 2029', version 1, published September 2024, read through a pdftotext rendering (content overview, assessment overview and objectives, all subject content, details of the assessment and the changes page). Exams in the June and November series. Check the headings and codes against the PDF.

This version is examined from 2027. A candidate sitting the examination in 2026 is examined on the previous syllabus (for exams up to 2026), which is not in the repository and has a different topic structure (for example Population and Migration were separate topics, Settlement dynamics and Production, location and change existed). Do not use this version for 2026 candidates.

Routes as printed: AS Level only (Papers 1 and 2 in one series; grades a-e); A Level staged over two years (AS in year 1, carried forward, then Papers 3 and 4, which must be taken in the same series); A Level in one series (all four papers; grades A*-E). Route A here covers both A Level routes.

Weightings: Papers 1 and 2 are 50% of AS Level and 25% of A Level each; Papers 3 and 4 are 25% of A Level each. weightingPercent records the A Level share; the AS shares are in each paper's description. Assessment objectives: AO1 Knowledge and understanding, AO2 Skills and analysis, AO3 Evaluation; the printed weightings table is partly overprinted in the copy read (AS Level about 53 / 35 / 12; A Level about 50 / 26 / 24 across the whole qualification): check it.

Paper structures as read: Paper 1 and Paper 2 (1 hour 30 minutes, 60 marks) each have Section A (all questions: one 15-mark structured question on each of the three topics, based on resources in an insert) and Section B (one 15-mark essay from a choice of three, one per topic); candidates write on the question paper. Paper 3 and Paper 4 (1 hour 30 minutes, 60 marks) each ask candidates to choose two of four topics; each chosen topic has one compulsory structured question worth 10 marks (resource-based) and one 20-mark essay from a choice of two; separate answer booklet. The overview page prints Section A as 45 marks and Section B as 15 marks, consistent with the details.

Detailed specific examples ('case studies') are not prescribed: teachers choose them, and the syllabus recommends examples from CE 2000 to the present. Where two contrasting countries are required, the syllabus suggests World Bank income groups. Writers choose real, dated, factual examples and label data with its source.

Topics 7-10 (Paper 3) and 11-14 (Paper 4) are optional groups: candidates choose two from each. The whole set is modelled so that every topic has content. Sub-topics 7.2 (weathering, 7.2.1, with granite landforms and karst), 8.1.3 (sub-aerial processes) and 10.2.1 (arid weathering) each deal with weathering; the shared weathering concept is covered once, at 7.2, and the coastal and arid applications sit in their own concepts.

Statistical tests, GIS and remote sensing are not part of the Cambridge content (the syllabus encourages GIS and technology in the classroom but states they are not used in exam papers; geography fieldwork is not assessed). Those concepts are ZIMSEC only.

The Cambridge syllabus gives no part marks or sub-question structure for the structured questions beyond the totals above; the structures used by our practice items are conventions a reviewer must check against the specimen papers.
overview: Cambridge International AS & A Level Geography (9696) is a two-stage course. The AS Level content has six topics: Paper 1 Physical Geography (hydrology, river processes and hazards; atmospheric processes and global climate change; Earth processes and mass movements) and Paper 2 Human Geography (population and migration; water resources and management; urban areas and management). The A Level adds two options from Paper 3 Global Environments (tropical, coastal, hazardous and arid environments) and two from Paper 4 Global Themes (climate change impacts and governance; environmental issues and management; trade, aid and tourism; disease and geography), with resource-based and evaluative essay skills and detailed specific examples throughout.
assessmentOverview: AS Level candidates take Paper 1 Physical Geography and Paper 2 Human Geography (each 1 hour 30 minutes, 60 marks: Section A three 15-mark structured questions, Section B one 15-mark essay from three). A Level candidates also take Paper 3 Global Environments and Paper 4 Global Themes (each 1 hour 30 minutes, 60 marks: two chosen topics, each with a compulsory 10-mark structured question and one 20-mark essay from two), either in the same series or later, carrying forward their AS result.

components.name: Paper 1: Physical Geography
components.description: Section A: three compulsory 15-mark resource-based structured questions, one per physical topic. Section B: one 15-mark essay from a choice of three. Answers on the question paper. 50% of AS Level, 25% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 2: Human Geography
components.description: Section A: three compulsory 15-mark resource-based structured questions, one per human topic. Section B: one 15-mark essay from a choice of three. Answers on the question paper. 50% of AS Level, 25% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 3: Global Environments
components.description: Two topics chosen from tropical, coastal, hazardous and arid environments; each has a compulsory 10-mark resource-based structured question and one 20-mark essay from a choice of two. Separate answer booklet. 25% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 4: Global Themes
components.description: Two topics chosen from climate change impacts and governance, environmental issues and management, trade, aid and tourism, and disease and geography; each has a compulsory 10-mark resource-based structured question and one 20-mark essay from a choice of two. Separate answer booklet. 25% of A Level.

routes.name: AS Level
routes.description: Papers 1 and 2 (grades a-e). Also the first year of the staged A Level route.

routes.name: A Level
routes.description: All four papers, in one series or staged (AS Level carried forward, then Papers 3 and 4 in the same series) (grades A*-E).

topics.name: AS Level subject content
topics.description: Topics 1-6: studied by all candidates; examined in Papers 1 (physical) and 2 (human) and assumed knowledge for Papers 3 and 4.

objectives.text: Describe the drainage basin as an open system with inputs, outputs, stores and transfers and how they relate.

Describe the movement of water: precipitation inputs; evaporation, evapotranspiration, condensation and channel-flow outputs; stores; and transfers such as stemflow, throughfall, infiltration, overland flow, throughflow, percolation and baseflow.
Explain how basin size, shape, drainage density, soils, rocks, vegetation, land use and climate influence the movement of water.
Read and interpret annual hydrographs and explain the factors behind variations in discharge through the year.
Identify the parts of a storm hydrograph and explain the factors that influence its shape.
Explain river erosion, load transport and deposition and the relationship between velocity, discharge and load size.
Describe river flow: velocity and discharge, laminar, turbulent and helicoidal flow, and the thalweg.
Explain the formation of meanders, riffles and pools, waterfalls, gorges, bluffs, floodplains and levees.
Explain the physical and human causes of river floods.
Describe the short- and long-term impacts of river floods and the factors of vulnerability.
Evaluate prediction, forecasting, warning, hard and soft engineering and emergency responses, with a detailed specific example of one recent river flood.

children.name: Atmospheric processes and global climate change
children.description: Candidates need an outline understanding of the vertical structure and composition of the atmosphere.

objectives.text: Explain energy budget systems: inputs, outputs, absorption, reflection, scattering, conduction, back radiation, latent and sensible heat.
Describe the global energy budget: latitudinal excesses and deficits and the natural greenhouse effect.
Explain atmospheric and oceanic transfers of energy: the tri-cellular model, ITCZ, wind belts, jet streams, ocean currents and gyres, and how they interact.
Explain seasonal variations in temperature, pressure and wind belts.
Compare daytime and night-time (diurnal) energy budgets.
Describe evaporation, condensation, freezing, melting and sublimation.
Explain convectional, frontal, orographic and radiation-cooling causes of precipitation.
Describe the types of precipitation: clouds, rain, hail, snow, dew and fog.

children.name: Global warming and climate change
children.description: Candidates need an outline understanding of climate change over the last 100 million years.

objectives.text: Evaluate the evidence for global warming and climate change: proxy records, temperature records since 1850, carbon dioxide, sea level, sea ice and glaciers.
Explain the causes: greenhouse gases and their global warming potential, natural factors (solar output, volcanoes, ENSO) and human factors, and the significance of the enhanced greenhouse effect.

children.name: Earth processes and mass movements
children.description: Candidates need an outline understanding of the structure of the Earth.

objectives.text: Compare continental and oceanic plates and describe plate movement.
Explain continental drift, geological and fossil evidence, sea-floor spreading and palaeomagnetism, convection currents, slab pull and ridge push.
Describe the global distribution of divergent, convergent (destructive), collision and conservative plate boundaries.
Describe faulting, rifting, sea-floor spreading, subduction, shearing and thrusting at each boundary type.
Explain the formation of fold mountains, volcanoes, mid-ocean ridges, ocean trenches, island arcs, fault scarps and rift valleys.
Describe heaves, flows, slides and falls.
Explain the physical and human causes of mass movement.
Evaluate prediction, slope stability measures and emergency responses, with a detailed specific example of one recent mass movement.
Describe global population distribution and density and the factors that influence them.
Explain trends in global population growth and their regional variations.
Explain natural increase and net migration, birth and death rates, TFR, IMR and life expectancy, and the factors that affect fertility and mortality.
Describe the components of population structure and interpret age-sex structure diagrams.
Critically evaluate the demographic transition model and explain the impacts of youthful and ageing populations.
Explain why governments manage natural increase and evaluate the population policies of two contrasting countries.
Distinguish voluntary, forced, temporary and permanent international migration.
Explain push and pull factors and the constraints on migration.
Evaluate the impacts of migration on source areas, destinations and migrants, with a detailed specific example of one country.

children.name: Water resources and management
children.description: Candidates need the drainage basin system from Topic 1.

objectives.text: Describe types of water resource and the global pattern of supply.
Explain the human water cycle and how human activities modify the water cycle.
Explain trends in water consumption, water stress and scarcity.

children.name: Factors influencing water resources at the regional/national scale

objectives.text: Explain the physical and human factors that influence the supply of water.
Explain the population, economic and seasonal factors that influence demand.
Explain water security and insecurity, access issues and the impact of drought.

children.name: Management of water resources at the regional/national scale

objectives.text: Evaluate strategies to increase water resources and access to water.
Evaluate strategies to manage demand for water.
Evaluate the challenges of managing water resources, with a detailed specific example from one country.
Describe processes of urban growth: urbanisation, suburbanisation, sprawl, counter-urbanisation, re-urbanisation and regeneration.
Explain the causes and consequences of urban growth for urban and rural areas.
Explain the hierarchy of urban areas, primate cities and world cities.
Explain the factors that influence urban structure and land-use zones, place identity and perception.
Explain the changing location of the CBD, retail, manufacturing, services and residential activities.
Explain the zonation of residential areas.
Explain the challenges of sustainability and the different views of groups of people.
Describe sustainability issues: waste, transport, housing, green space and water.
Evaluate strategies for the sustainable management of urban areas, with a detailed specific example of one urban area.

topics.name: A Level subject content
topics.description: Topics 7-14: A Level candidates study all the AS Level content and choose two of the four Paper 3 topics (7-10) and two of the four Paper 4 topics (11-14).

objectives.text: Describe the global distribution of humid tropical (rainforest) and seasonally humid tropical (savanna) environments.
Describe their climates, including monsoons, annual and diurnal variations.
Explain the distribution and climate using the ITCZ, subtropical anticyclones, monsoons and ENSO.

children.name: Processes and landforms in tropical environments

objectives.text: Explain chemical, physical and biological weathering processes in tropical environments.
Describe and explain granite landforms: bornhardts (dwala, ruware), kopjes and tors.
Describe and explain tropical karst: cone, tower and cockpit karst.

children.name: Vegetation, soils and ecosystems in tropical environments

objectives.text: Explain the development of plant communities in rainforest and savanna and the effects of climate and people.
Describe tropical soil-forming processes, soil types and profiles.
Explain nutrient cycling using Gersmehl diagrams and the effects of burning, clearing and deforestation.

children.name: Changes and challenges in tropical environments

objectives.text: Explain population pressure, exploitation and climate-change challenges for tropical environments.
Evaluate management strategies in a detailed specific example of one rainforest or savanna ecosystem.
Explain the factors influencing coastal environments: waves, rock type and structure, climate and human activity.
Describe marine erosion processes.
Describe sub-aerial weathering and mass movement on coasts.
Explain marine transportation and deposition, longshore drift and sediment cells.

children.name: Characteristics and formation of coastal landforms

objectives.text: Explain the role of coastal processes in forming and shaping landforms.
Describe and explain erosional landforms and concordant and discordant coastlines.
Describe and explain beaches, spits, tombolos and barrier beaches.
Explain the formation of sand dunes, saltmarshes and mangrove swamps.

children.name: Coral reefs
children.description: Candidates need a basic understanding of what coral is, its slow growth and the importance of reefs.

objectives.text: Describe the distribution of coral reefs and the conditions for coral growth.
Explain the threats to coral reefs and evaluate management strategies.

children.name: Physical and human challenges to the coastal environment

objectives.text: Evaluate hard and soft engineering management strategies in a detailed specific example of a stretch of coastline.

children.name: Earthquake and volcanic hazards and impacts

objectives.text: Describe the global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes and the related plate boundaries.
Explain the severity, hazards, vulnerability and impacts of earthquakes.
Explain volcano formation, types, eruption styles, hazards, the VEI, vulnerability and impacts.
Evaluate prediction, risk perception, design and planning, and emergency response and recovery.
Explain the distribution, conditions, formation and strength scale of tropical cyclones.
Describe the hazards, vulnerability, impacts and climate-change links.
Evaluate prediction, warning and management strategies.
Describe the global distribution of wildfire risk and the physical and human causes.
Explain wildfire spread, vulnerability, impacts and climate-change effects.
Evaluate prediction and management of wildfires.
Evaluate management of two or more hazards in a detailed specific example of one multi-hazard environment.
Describe the global distribution of hot arid and hot semi-arid environments.
Describe their climatic characteristics.
Explain the causes of aridity.

children.name: Processes and landforms in arid environments

objectives.text: Explain physical and chemical weathering in arid environments.
Explain wind erosion, transportation and deposition.
Explain fluvial processes, episodic rainfall, sheet floods and flash floods.
Describe and explain wind and water erosional and depositional landforms.

children.name: Vegetation and soils in arid environments

objectives.text: Describe vegetation characteristics and plant adaptations to extreme temperatures and drought.
Describe soil-forming processes and the characteristics of solonetz and solonchaks.

children.name: Changes and challenges in arid environments

objectives.text: Explain population pressure, desertification and climate-change challenges.
Evaluate management strategies in a detailed specific example of one arid or semi-arid environment.

children.name: Climate change impacts and governance
children.description: Paper 4 option (choose two of topics 11-14). Topic 2.3 is assumed knowledge. Candidates need only an outline knowledge of the IPCC; details of RCPs and SSPs are not required.

objectives.text: Interpret the five categories of projected climate change in terms of warming, emissions, peak and net-zero years, and their impacts on sea level, precipitation and extreme weather.
Explain climate change impacts on cold and marine environments.
Explain feedback loops, tipping points and their possible effects.
Describe the global socio-economic impacts of climate change and their distribution.
Explain patterns of human vulnerability and the groups the IPCC identifies as most vulnerable.

children.name: Governance of climate change
children.description: Candidates need an outline knowledge of the UNFCCC and COP meetings and their links to the IPCC.

objectives.text: Describe the Paris Agreement and major agreements since 2015.
Evaluate mitigation and adaptation strategies and the challenges of implementing them.
Compare the management strategies of two countries (detailed specific examples), including justice issues.
Describe energy resources used to produce electricity and domestic fuels, their uses and issues, and global patterns and trends.
Explain the challenges of the transition from fossil fuels to sustainable energy.
Explain the national factors that affect the balance between energy sources.
Evaluate electricity production and energy security in two contrasting countries (detailed specific examples).

children.name: Pollution and environmental degradation in rural areas

objectives.text: Explain how mining and quarrying, agriculture and large infrastructure projects cause pollution and degradation.
Evaluate sustainable practices in extraction and agriculture, monitoring and legislation.
Evaluate a detailed specific example of environmental degradation in one rural area.

children.name: Pollution and environmental degradation in urban areas

objectives.text: Explain the factors and sources of pollution and degradation in urban environments in LICs, MICs and HICs.
Evaluate sustainable practices in domestic environments, construction, energy, transport and waste management.
Explain the reasons for urban planning and controls.
Evaluate a detailed specific example of environmental degradation in one urban area.
Describe flows and patterns of visible trade and inequalities in volume and value.
Explain the physical, historical, economic and political factors influencing trade patterns.
Compare two contrasting countries' trade, one dependent on primary commodity exports (detailed specific examples).

children.name: International organisations involved in trade and aid

objectives.text: Explain the role and impact of the WTO and UNCTAD on global trade flows.
Evaluate types of international aid and the roles of NGOs and IGOs.
Describe patterns and trends in international tourism and the factors behind them.
Evaluate the economic, social and environmental impacts of tourism and the issues of sustainability.
Evaluate tourism development and management in two contrasting tourist areas or resorts (detailed specific examples).

children.name: Disease and geography
children.description: Paper 4 option (choose two of topics 11-14). The focus is on the environmental, social, economic and political aspects of disease, not the medical and biological detail.

objectives.text: Use terms for the spread and impact of disease: outbreak, epidemic, pandemic, endemic, prevalence, morbidity, death rate, IMR, life expectancy, GDP and healthcare spending.
Explain the spatial variation in disease and in causes of death between LICs, MICs and HICs.

children.name: Pathogenic diseases, their spread and impacts

objectives.text: Explain the transmission, distribution and impacts of influenza and one country's control strategies.
Explain the transmission, distribution and impacts of cholera and one country's control strategies.
Explain the transmission, distribution and impacts of malaria and one country's control strategies.

children.name: Monitoring and response to pathogenic diseases

objectives.text: Explain the factors in effective disease monitoring and the controls of disease.
Explain the factors in an effective response to outbreaks.
Compare two contrasting countries' responses to one pandemic since 2000.
Critically evaluate a global programme to eradicate one pathogenic disease.

topics.name: Geographical skills
topics.description: Skills used throughout the course and in every paper. Fieldwork and geographical investigations are encouraged but not assessed; GIS and technology are encouraged but not used in exam papers.

objectives.text: Interpret survey map extracts (1:25 000 and 1:50 000), thematic and distribution maps and sketch maps.
Interpret photographs and satellite images, graphs and diagrams, written extracts and numeric data, and recognise their limitations.
Plan and carry out small-scale fieldwork or a classroom-based investigation and collect primary data (not assessed).
Evaluate the reliability and limitations of data collected.
Respond to the command words (describe, explain, assess, evaluate, compare, suggest and others) in structured questions and essays.
Present a logical, structured, evidence-based argument supported by examples and a conclusion.
